entries.0df582aa9bc844d8801302aad8b366a29d62e6a8: <div sID="gen12243" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="98" osisID="Ps.98" sID="Ps.98"/> <div eID="gen12243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12244" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12245" type="x-p"/> This psalm is to the same purport with the <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13 Ps.97.1-Ps.97.12">two foregoing psalms</reference>; it is a prophecy of the kingdom of the Messiah, the settling of it up in the world, and the bringing of the Gentiles into it. The Chaldee entitles it a prophetic psalm. It sets forth, I. The glory of the Redeemer, <reference osisRef="Ps.98.1-Ps.98.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. The joy of the redeemed, <reference osisRef="Ps.98.4-Ps.98.9">ver. 4-9</reference>. If we in a right manner give to Christ this glory, and upon right grounds take to ourselves this joy, in singing this psalm, we sing it with understanding. If those who saw Christ's triumph thus, much more reason have we to do so who see these things accomplished and share in the better things provided for us, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.40">Heb. xi. 40</reference>.
entries.36d79a78dbf9f4557bd4467210d5c7ac877742fe: <div eID="gen12245" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12244" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">An Invitation to Praise.</title> <div sID="gen12246" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> O sing unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> a new song; for he hath done marvellous things: his right hand, and his holy arm, hath gotten him the victory. <hi type="super">2</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath made known his salvation: his righteousness hath he openly showed in the sight of the heathen. <hi type="super">3</hi> He hath remembered his mercy and his truth toward the house of Israel: all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God. <div eID="gen12246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12247" type="x-p"/> We are here called upon again to <hi type="italic">sing unto the Lord a new song,</hi> as before, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1">Ps. xcvi. 1</reference>. "Sing a most excellent song, the best song you have." Let the song of Christ's love be like Solomon's on that subject, a <hi type="italic">song of songs.</hi> A song of praise for redeeming love is a <hi type="italic">new song,</hi> such a song as had not been sung before; for this is a mystery which was hidden from ages and generations. Converts sing a <hi type="italic">new song,</hi> very different from what they had sung; they change their wonder and change their joy, and therefore change their note. If the grace of God put a new heart into our breasts, it will therewith put a new song into our mouths. In the new Jerusalem there will be new songs sung, that will be new to eternity, and never wax old. Let this new song be sung to the praise of God, in consideration of these four things:— <div eID="gen12247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12248" type="x-p"/> I. The wonders he has wrought: <hi type="italic">He has done marvellous things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.98.1">v. 1</reference>. Note, The work of our salvation by Christ is a work of wonder. If we take a view of all the steps of it from the contrivance of it, and the counsels of God concerning it before all time, to the consummation of it, and its everlasting consequences when time shall be no more, we shall say, God has in it <hi type="italic">done marvellous things;</hi> it is all his doing and it is <hi type="italic">marvellous in our eyes.</hi> The more it is known the more it will be admired. <div eID="gen12248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12249" type="x-p"/> II. The conquests he has won: <hi type="italic">His right hand and his holy arm have gotten him the victory.</hi> Our Redeemer has surmounted all the difficulties that lay in the way of our redemption, has broken through them all, and was not discouraged by the services or sufferings appointed him. He has subdued all the enemies that opposed it, has gotten the victory over Satan, disarmed him, and cast him out of his strong-holds, has <hi type="italic">spoiled principalities and powers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col. ii. 15</reference>), has <hi type="italic">taken the prey from the mighty</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.24">Isa. xlix. 24</reference>), and given death his death's wound. He has gotten a clear and complete victory, not only for himself, but for us also, for we through him are more than conquerors. He got this victory by his own power; there was <hi type="italic">none to help, none to uphold,</hi> none that durst venture into the service; but his <hi type="italic">right hand and his holy arm,</hi> which are always stretched out with good success, because they are never stretched out but in a good cause, these have <hi type="italic">gotten him the victory,</hi> have <hi type="italic">brought him relief or deliverance.</hi> God's power and faithfulness, called here <hi type="italic">his right hand and his holy arm,</hi> brought relief to the Lord Jesus, in raising him from the dead, and exalting him personally to the right hand of God; so Dr. Hammond. <div eID="gen12249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12250" type="x-p"/> III. The discoveries he has made to the world of the work of redemption. What he has wrought for us he has revealed to us, and both by his Son; the gospel-revelation is that on which the gospel-kingdom is founded—<hi type="italic">the word which God sent,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.10.36">Acts x. 36</reference>. The <hi type="italic">opening of the sealed book</hi> is that which is to be celebrated with songs of praise (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.8">Rev. v. 8</reference>), because by it was brought to light the mystery which had long been hid in God. Observe, 1. The subject of this discovery—his salvation and his righteousness, <reference osisRef="Ps.98.3">v. 3</reference>. Righteousness and salvation are often put together; as <reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Isa. lxi. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.13">xlvi. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.5-Isa.51.6 Isa.51.8">li. 5, 6, 8</reference>. Salvation denotes the redemption itself, and righteousness the way in which it was wrought, by the righteousness of Christ. Or the salvation includes all our gospel-privileges and the righteousness all our gospel-duties; both are made known, for God has joined them together, and we must not separate them. Or righteousness is here put for the way of our justification by Christ, which is revealed in the gospel to be by faith, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.17">Rom. i. 17</reference>. 2. The plainness of this discovery. He has openly shown it, not in types and figures as under the law, but it is written as with a sunbeam, that he that runs may read it. Ministers are appointed to preach it with all plainness of speech. 3. The extent of this discovery. It is made in the sight of the heathen, and not of the Jews only: <hi type="italic">All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God;</hi> for to the Gentiles was the word of salvation sent. <div eID="gen12250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12251" type="x-p"/> IV. The accomplishment of the prophecies and promises of the Old Testament, in this (<reference osisRef="Ps.98.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">He has remembered his mercy and his truth towards the house of Israel.</hi> God had mercy in store for the seed of Abraham, and had given them many and great assurances of the kindness he designed them in the latter days; and it was in pursuance of all those that he raised up his Son Jesus to be not only a <hi type="italic">light to lighten the Gentiles,</hi> but <hi type="italic">the glory of his people Israel;</hi> for he sent him, in the first place, to bless <hi type="italic">them.</hi> God is said, in sending Christ, to <hi type="italic">perform the mercy promised to our fathers, and to remember the holy covenant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.72">Luke i. 72</reference>. It was in consideration of that, and not of their merit.
entries.c1428008be47e0a3a4523c1580a0169b34efd1b0: <div eID="gen12251" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">An Invitation to Praise.</title> <div sID="gen12252" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Make a joyful noise unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , all the earth: make a loud noise, and rejoice, and sing praise. <hi type="super">5</hi> Sing unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with the harp; with the harp, and the voice of a psalm. <hi type="super">6</hi> With trumpets and sound of cornet make a joyful noise before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the King. <hi type="super">7</hi> Let the sea roar, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein. <hi type="super">8</hi> Let the floods clap <hi type="italic">their</hi> hands: let the hills be joyful together <hi type="super">9</hi> Before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; for he cometh to judge the earth: with righteousness shall he judge the world, and the people with equity. <div eID="gen12252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12253" type="x-p"/> The setting up of the kingdom of Christ is here represented as a matter of joy and praise. <div eID="gen12253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12254" type="x-p"/> I. Let all the children of men rejoice in it, for they all have, or may have, benefit by it. Again and again we are here called upon by all ways and means possible to express our joy in it and give God praise for it: <hi type="italic">Make a joyful noise,</hi> as before, <reference osisRef="Ps.95.1-Ps.95.2">Ps. xcv. 1, 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Make a loud noise,</hi> as those that are affected with those glad tidings and are desirous to affect others with them. <hi type="italic">Rejoice and sing praise,</hi> sing <hi type="italic">Hosannas</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.9">Matt. xxi. 9</reference>), sing <hi type="italic">Hallelujahs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.6">Rev. xix. 6</reference>. Let him be welcomed to the throne, as new kings are, with acclamations of joy and loud shouts, till the earth ring again, as when Solomon was proclaimed, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.40">1 Kings i. 40</reference>. And let the shouts of the crowd be accompanied with the <hi type="italic">singers and players on instruments</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.87.7">Ps. lxxvii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.25">lxvi. 25</reference>), as is usual in such solemnities. 1. Let sacred songs attend the new King: "<hi type="italic">Sing praise, sing with the voice of a psalm.</hi> Express your joy; thus proclaim it, thus excite it yet more, and thus propagate it among others." 2. Let these be assisted with sacred music, not only with the soft and gentle melody of <hi type="italic">the harp,</hi> but since it is a victorious King whose glory is to be celebrated, who goes forth conquering and to conquer, let him be proclaimed with the martial sound of the <hi type="italic">trumpet</hi> and <hi type="italic">cornet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.98.6">v. 6</reference>. Let all this joy be directed to God, and expressed in a solemn religious manner: <hi type="italic">Make a joyful noise to the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.98.4">v. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Sing to the Lord,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.98.5">v. 5</reference>); do it <hi type="italic">before the Lord, the King,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.98.6">v. 6</reference>. Carnal mirth is an enemy to this holy joy. When David danced before the ark he pleaded that <hi type="italic">it was before the Lord;</hi> and the piety and devotion of the intention not only vindicated what he did, but commended it. We must rejoice <hi type="italic">before the Lord</hi> whenever we draw near to him (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.12">Deut. xii. 12</reference>), before <hi type="italic">the Lord Jesus,</hi> and before him, not only as the Saviour, but as the King, the King of kings, the church's King, and our King. <div eID="gen12254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12255" type="x-p"/> II. Let the inferior creatures rejoice in it, <reference osisRef="Ps.98.7-Ps.98.9">v. 7-9</reference>. This is to the same purport with what we had before (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.11-Ps.96.13">Ps. xcvi. 11-13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let the sea roar,</hi> and let that be called, not as it used to be, a <hi type="italic">dreadful noise,</hi> but a <hi type="italic">joyful noise;</hi> for the coming of Christ, and the salvation wrought out by him, have quite altered the property of the troubles and terrors of this world, so that when the floods <hi type="italic">lift up their voice, lift up their waves,</hi> we must not construe that to be the sea roaring against us, but rather rejoicing with us. Let the <hi type="italic">floods</hi> express their joy, as men do when they <hi type="italic">clap their hands;</hi> and let the hills, that trembled for fear before God when he came down to give the law at Mount Sinai, dance for joy before him when his gospel is preached and that word of the Lord goes forth from Zion in a still small voice: <hi type="italic">Let the hills be joyful together before the Lord.</hi> This intimates that the kingdom of Christ would be a blessing to the whole creation; but that, as the inferior creatures declare the glory of the Creator (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.1">Ps. xix. 1</reference>), so they declare the glory of the Redeemer, for by him all things not only subsist in their being, but consist in their order. It intimates likewise that the children of men would be wanting in paying their due respects to the Redeemer, and therefore that he must look for his honour from the sea and the floods, which would shame the stupidity and ingratitude of mankind. And perhaps respect is here had to the <hi type="italic">new heavens</hi> and the <hi type="italic">new earth,</hi> which we yet, according to his promise, look for (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.13">2 Pet. iii. 13</reference>), and this second mention of his coming (after the like, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13">Ps. xcvi.</reference>) may principally refer to his second coming, when all these things shall be so dissolved as to be refined; then shall he come to <hi type="italic">judge the world with righteousness.</hi> In the prospect of that day all that are sanctified do rejoice, and even the sea, and the floods, and the hills, would rejoice if they could. One would think that Virgil had these psalms in his eye, as well as the oracles of the Cumean Sibyl, in his fourth eclogue, where he either ignorantly or basely applies to Asinius Pollio the ancient prophecies, which at that time were expected to be fulfilled; for he lived in the reign of Augustus Cæsar, a little before our Saviour's birth. He owns they looked for the birth of a child from heaven that should be a great blessing to the world, and restore the golden age:— <div eID="gen12255" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen12256"/> <l level="1" sID="gen12257"/>Jam nova progenies c&#339;lo demittitur alto—<l eID="gen12257" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen12258"/>A new race descends from the lofty sky;<l eID="gen12258" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen12259"/>Te duce, si qua manent sceleris vestigia nostri,<l eID="gen12259" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen12260"/>Irrita perpetua solvent formidine terras—<l eID="gen12260" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen12261"/>Thy influence shall efface every stain of corruption,<l eID="gen12261" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen12262"/>And free the world from alarm.<l eID="gen12262" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen12256"/> <div sID="gen12263" type="x-p"/> Many other things he says of this long-looked-for child, which Ludovicus Vives, in his notes on that eclogue, thinks applicable to Christ; and he concludes, as the psalmist here, with a prospect of the rejoicing of the whole creation herein:— <div eID="gen12263" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen12264"/> <l level="1" sID="gen12265"/>Aspice, venturo lætentur ut omnia sæclo—<l eID="gen12265" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen12266"/>See how this promis'd age makes all rejoice. <l eID="gen12266" level="1"/><lg eID="gen12264"/> <chapter eID="Ps.98"/>

entries.67bfd3ad38279f859027402b1378ac2c1ac1d303: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6633"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 98</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.98.1-Ps.98.9">Psa 98:1-9</reference>. In view of the wonders of grace and righteousness displayed in God's salvation, the whole creation is invited to unite in praise.</title> <div sID="gen10155" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6633"/><hi type="bold">1. gotten ... victory--</hi>literally, "made salvation," enabled Him to save His people.<div eID="gen10155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10156" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">right hand, and ... arm--</hi>denote power.<div eID="gen10156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10157" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holy arm--</hi>or, "arm of holiness," the power of His united moral perfections (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.3">Psa 22:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.11">32:11</reference>). <div eID="gen10157" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b9122de258fcc665921fab29867f2ab393d667d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6634"/><div sID="gen10158" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6634"/><hi type="bold">2. salvation--</hi>the result of His righteousness (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.17">Psa 7:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.1">31:1</reference>), and both are publicly displayed. <div eID="gen10158" type="x-p"/>
entries.b6f7e208c6a1eecd5a68615c389c0d0803f35ae4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6635"/><div sID="gen10159" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6635"/>3. The union of mercy and truth (<reference osisRef="Ps.57.3">Psa 57:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.85.10">85:10</reference>) secure the blessings of the promise (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Ge 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.18.18">18:18</reference>) to all the world (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.10">Is 52:10</reference>). <div eID="gen10159" type="x-p"/>
entries.dfb1d5ca6dffb2e04e2a9f701a40b9817ed37fec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6636"/><div sID="gen10160" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6636"/><hi type="bold">4-6. make a loud noise--</hi>or, "burst forth" (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.7">Is 14:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.23">44:23</reference>).<div eID="gen10160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before ... King--</hi>hail Him as your sovereign; and while, with every aid to demonstrate zeal and joy, intelligent creatures are invited to praise, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.96.11-Ps.96.13">Psa 96:11-13</reference>, inanimate nature is also summoned to honor Him who triumphs and rules in righteousness and equity. <chapter eID="Ps.98"/>

entries.688334b5251fcc1fd6059eb025888512057b767a: <div eID="gen21862" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21863" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21864" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21864" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21863" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21865" type="x-p"/> God is celebrated for his wondrous works, <reference osisRef="Psa.98.1">Psa 98:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.98.2">Psa 98:2</reference>; for the exact fulfillment of his gracious promises, <reference osisRef="Psa.98.3">Psa 98:3</reference>. The manner in which he is to be praised, <reference osisRef="Psa.98.4-Psa.98.6">Psa 98:4-6</reference>. Inanimate creation called to bear a part in this concert, <reference osisRef="Psa.98.7">Psa 98:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.98.8">Psa 98:8</reference>. The justice of his judgments, <reference osisRef="Psa.98.9">Psa 98:9</reference>. <div eID="gen21865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21866" type="x-p"/> In the Hebrew this is simply termed מזמור mizmor, a Psalm. In the Chaldee, A prophetic Psalm. In the Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, A Psalm of David. In the Syriac it is attributed to David, and stated to be composed concerning the "Restoration of the Israelites from Egypt; but is to be understood spiritually of the advent of the Messiah, and the vocation of the Gentiles to the Christian faith." <div eID="gen21866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21867" type="x-p"/> The Psalm in its subject is very like the ninety-sixth. It was probably written to celebrate the deliverance from the Babylonish captivity; but is to be understood prophetically of the redemption of the world by Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen21867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21868" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21869" type="x-p"/> A new song - A song of excellence. Give him the highest praise. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.96.1">Psa 96:1</reference> (note). <div eID="gen21869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21870" type="x-p"/> Hath done marvellous things - נפלאות niphlaoth, "miracles," the same word as in <reference osisRef="Psa.96.3">Psa 96:3</reference>, where we translate it wonders. <div eID="gen21870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21871" type="x-p"/> His holy arm - His Almighty power: - <div eID="gen21871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21872" type="x-p"/> Hath gotten him the victory - הושיעה לו hoshiah llo, "hath made salvation to himself."
entries.addcdeb5ba9ca89175a00d9c126d08db7faab915: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21873" type="x-p"/> Made known his salvation - He has delivered his people in such a way as to show that it was supernatural, and that their confidence in the unseen God was not in vain.
entries.0f750217426030ff6e1bbf13bf0759cb15126888: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21874" type="x-p"/> He hath remembered his mercy - His gracious promises to their forefathers. <div eID="gen21874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21875" type="x-p"/> And his truth - Faithfully accomplishing what he had promised. All this was fulfilled under the Gospel.
entries.23dcb90c9b22448ddaaeb5d39073a6c70b692b8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21876" type="x-p"/> With - the voice of a Psalm - I think זמרה zimrah, which we translate Psalm, means either a musical instrument, or a species of ode modulated by different voices.
entries.7e10e6b2a422f306108f8c06ed90aa81ca275a7d: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21877" type="x-p"/> With trumpets - חצצרות chatsotseroth. Some kind of tubular instruments, of the form and management of which we know nothing. <div eID="gen21877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21878" type="x-p"/> And sound of cornet - שופר shophar, the word commonly used for what we call trumpet.
entries.6dd0c9e1cf197e3ce0ca1bd88fff14cd3426f22f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21879" type="x-p"/> Let the sea roar - These are either fine poetic images; or, if we take them as referring to the promulgation of the Gospel, by the sea all maritime countries and commercial nations may be intended.
entries.ed79db9f1b4345ebef61e37b241b64a13003e450: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21880" type="x-p"/> Let the floods clap their hands - נהרות neharoth, properly the rivers - possibly meaning immense continents, where only large rivers are found; thus including inland people, as well as maritime stations, and those on the sea-coasts generally; as in those early times little more than the coasts of the sea were known. The Gospel shall be preached in the most secluded nations of the world. <div eID="gen21880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21881" type="x-p"/> Let the hills be joyful - All the inhabitants of rocky and mountainous countries.
entries.db297570760fa8a672d88e22847acc80da73d1ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21882" type="x-p"/> For he cometh to judge the earth - He comes to make known his salvation, and show his merciful designs to all the children of men. <div eID="gen21882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21883" type="x-p"/> With righteousness shall he judge the world - His word shall not be confined; all shall know him, from the least to the greatest: he shall show that he is loving to every man, and hateth nothing that he hath made. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Psa.96.1-Psa.96.13">Psa 96:1-13</reference> (note). There is a very great similarity between this Psalm and the Song or Magnificat of the Blessed Virgin. I shall note some of the parallels, chiefly from Bishop Nicholson. <div eID="gen21883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21884" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is an evident prophecy of Christ's coming to save the world; and what is here foretold by David is, in the Blessed Virgin's song, chanted forth as being accomplished. David is the Voice, and Mary is the Echo. <div eID="gen21884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21885" type="x-p"/> 1. David "O sing unto the Lord a new song." (The Voice). Mary "My soul doth magnify the Lord." (The Echo). <div eID="gen21885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21886" type="x-p"/> 2. David "He hath done marvellous things." (The Voice). Mary "He that is mighty hath done great things." (The Echo). <div eID="gen21886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21887" type="x-p"/> 3. David "With his own right hand and holy arm hath he gotten himself the victory." (The Voice). Mary "He hath showed strength with his arm and scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts." (The Echo). <div eID="gen21887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21888" type="x-p"/> 4. David "The Lord hath made known his salvation; his righteousness hath he openly showed," etc. (The Voice). Mary "His mercy is on them that fear him, from generation to generation." (The Echo). <div eID="gen21888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21889" type="x-p"/> 5. David "He hath remembered his mercy and his truth toward the house of Israel." (The Voice). Mary "He hath holpen his servant Israel in remembrance of his mercy." (The Echo). <div eID="gen21889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21890" type="x-p"/> These parallels are very striking; and it seems as if Mary had this Psalm in her eye when she composed her song of triumph. And this is a farther argument that the whole Psalm, whether it record the deliverance of Israel from Egypt, or the Jews from the Babylonish captivity, is yet to be ultimately understood of the redemption of the world by Jesus Christ, and the proclamation of his Gospel through all the nations of the earth: and taken in this view, no language can be too strong, nor poetic imagery too high, to point out the unsearchable riches of Christ.  <chapter eID="Ps.98"/> <div eID="gen21890" type="x-p"/>

entries.7bad9e87a98325594f7d9dd46ceff51ab949a046: <div eID="gen9957" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Greeting to Him Who Is Become Known in Righteousness and Salvation</title> <div sID="gen9958" type="x-p"/> This is the only Psalm which is inscribed מזמור without further addition, whence it is called in <hi type="italic">B. Aboda Zara</hi>, 24 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, מזמורא יתומא (the orphan Psalm). The Peshîto Syriac inscribes it <hi type="italic">De redemtione populi ex Aegypto</hi>; the “new song,” however, is not the song of Moses, but the counterpart of this, cf. Rev 15:3. There “the Lord reigneth” resounded for the first time, at the sea; here the completion of the beginning there commenced is sung, viz., the final glory of the divine kingdom, which through judgment breaks through to its full reality. The beginning and end are taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1">Psa 96:1</reference>-13. Almost all that lies between is taken from the second part of Isaiah. This book of consolation for the exiles is become as it were a Castalian spring for the religious lyric.
entries.daddf6f85e8b08ff0a067edc32d430d3543dfb3a: <reference osisRef="Ps.98.1-Ps.98.3">Psa 98:1-3</reference> <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.98.1">Psa 98:1</reference></hi> we have already read in Psa 96:1. What follows in <reference osisRef="Ps.98.1">Psa 98:1</reference> is taken from <reference osisRef="Isa.52.10">Isa 52:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">Isa 63:5</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.98.7">Psa 98:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.16">Psa 59:16</reference>, cf. Psa 40:10. The primary passage, <reference osisRef="Isa.52.10">Isa 52:10</reference>, shows that the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi> of <reference osisRef="Ps.98.2">Psa 98:2</reference> is correctly placed. לעיני is the opposite of hearsay (cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">l - l - ‛yn</hi>, from one’s own observation, <hi type="italic">opp</hi>. Arab. <hi type="italic">l - l - chbr</hi>, from the narrative of another person). The dative לבית ישראל depends upon ויּזכּר, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.106.45">Psa 106:45</reference>, cf. Luk 1:54.
entries.20d34b01b66c1eda8576955423b8ec56098d5d45: <reference osisRef="Ps.98.4-Ps.98.6">Psa 98:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen9958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9959" type="x-p"/> The call in <reference osisRef="Ps.98.4">Psa 98:4</reference> demands some joyful manifestation of the mouth, which can be done in many ways; in <reference osisRef="Ps.98.5">Psa 98:5</reference> the union of song and the music of stringed instruments, as of the Levites; and in <reference osisRef="Ps.98.6">Psa 98:6</reference> the sound of wind instruments, as of the priests. On <reference osisRef="Ps.98.4">Psa 98:4</reference> cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.44.23">Isa 44:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.13">Isa 49:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.9">Isa 52:9</reference>, together with <reference osisRef="Isa.14.7">Isa 14:7</reference> (inasmuch as פּצחוּ ורננוּ is equivalent to פּצחוּ רנּה). קול זמרה is found also in Isa 51:3.
entries.1aa9ec06c71eb8050f9fc1329e6327db331aad5c: <reference osisRef="Ps.98.7-Ps.98.9">Psa 98:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen9959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9960" type="x-p"/> Here, too, it is all an echo of the earlier language of Psalms and prophets: <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.98.7">Psa 98:7</reference></hi> = <reference osisRef="Ps.96.11">Psa 96:11</reference>; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.98.7">Psa 98:7</reference></hi> like <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1">Psa 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.98.8">Psa 98:8</reference> after <reference osisRef="Isa.55.12">Isa 55:12</reference> (where we find מחא כּף instead of the otherwise customary תּקע כּף, <reference osisRef="Ps.47.2">Psa 47:2</reference>; or הכּה כּף, 2Ki 11:12, is said of the trees of the field); <reference osisRef="Ps.98.9">Psa 98:9</reference> - <reference osisRef="Ps.96.13">Psa 96:13</reference>, cf. Psa 36:10. In the bringing in of nature to participate in the joy of mankind, the clapping rivers (נהרות) are original to this Psalm: the rivers cast up high waves, which flow into one another like clapping hands;<note placement="foot">Luther renders: “the water-floods exult” (<hi type="italic">frohlocken</hi>); and <hi type="italic">Eychman’s Vocabularius</hi> predicantium explains <hi type="italic">plaudere</hi> by “to exult (<hi type="italic">frohlocken</hi>) for joy, to smite the hands together <hi type="italic">prae gaudio</hi>;” cf. Luther’s version of Eze 21:17.</note> cf. <reference osisRef="Hab.3.10">Hab 3:10</reference>, where the abyss of the sea lifts up its hands on high, i.e., causes its waves to run mountain-high.  <chapter eID="Ps.98"/> <div eID="gen9960" type="x-p"/>

entries.282636409a4342ff69b6ce1d7025dedf2a1b26ca:
PSALM 98
This psalm has a great resemblance to the ninety-sixth, not only in matter, but language. The great scope of it is to show that the glory of God would be illustriously displayed in the spread of the knowledge of his name throughout the world, both from the more ample fulfillment which would be given upon the manifestation of the Savior, to the promises made to the posterity of Abraham, and from the sudden extension of salvation to all parts of the earth. He calls upon men to magnify the name of God on this account.
Psalm 98:1-3
1. Sing unto Jehovah a new song, for he hath done marvelous things: his own right hand, and the arm of his holiness, hath gotten him the victory.
The last clause is “literally, have wrought deliverance for him, i e., not deliverance of him, as if God had been himself in danger or distress; but that is done for any one, which is done agreeably to his wishes and intentions, and at his instigation. The original, therefore, expresses, that the deliverance wrought was originally designed and decreed by God, and that his immediate power effected the thing intended without any other aid.” — Horsley Street translates, “hath wrought salvation for us.” He thinks that instead of לו, for him, we should read לנו, for us
2. Jehovah hath made known his salvation: his righteousness he hath revealed in the sight of the heathen. 3. He hath remembered his goodness and truth towards the house of Israel: all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.
The last part of this verse is in the same words with Isaiah 52:10.
 
1 Sing unto Jehovah a new song I have already remarked, that the expression here used denotes an extraordinary, not a common, ascription of praise. This appears from the reason assigned for it, That God had manifested his salvation in a singular and incredible manner. For having spoken of marvelous things, he represents this as the sum of all, that God had procured salvation with his own right hand;
“Car apres avoir parle des miracles, il les restreint specialement a une somme, ascavoir, que Dieu s’est acquis salut par sa propre vertu.” — Fr.
that is, not by human means, or in an ordinary way, but delivering his Church in an unprecedented manner. Isaiah enlarges upon this miracle of God’s power:
“The Lord looked if there were any to help, and wondered that there was no intercessor: therefore his own arm brought salvation, and his righteousness sustained him,” (Isaiah 59:16)
In both passages the arm of God stands opposed to ordinary means, which although when employed they derogate nothing from the glory of God, yet prevent us from so fully discovering his presence as we might otherwise do. The language of the Psalmist amounts to a declaration that God would not save the world by means of an ordinary kind, but would come forth himself and show that he was the author of a salvation in every respect so singular. He reasonably infers that mercy of such a wonderful, and, to us, incomprehensible kind, should be celebrated by no ordinary measures of praise. This is brought out still more clearly in the verse which follows, where it is said that his salvation and righteousness are shown to the nations What could have been less looked for than that light should have arisen upon these dark and benighted places, and that righteousness should have appeared in the habitations of desperate wickedness? Salvation is mentioned first, although it is, properly speaking, the effect of righteousness. Such an inversion of the natural order is often observed in stating divine benefits; nor is it surprising that what is the means, and should be mentioned first, is sometimes set last, and follows by way of explanation. I may add, that the righteousness of God, which is the source of salvation, does not consist in his recompensing men according to their works, but is just the illustration of his mercy, grace, and faithfulness.
